Input: Has Einstein's general relativity been proven by any experiments? Is it still considered a theory until proven by an experiment? First, let me clarify the meaning of the word, “theory”. Hint: It’s not about idle theorizing. Here’s the definition from the American Heritage Dictionary: theory (thê´e-rê, thîr´ê) noun plural theories 1. a. Systematically organized knowledge applicable in a relatively wide variety of circumstances, especially a system of assumptions, accepted principles, and rules of procedure devised to analyze, predict, or otherwise explain the nature or behavior of a specified set of phenomena. b. Such knowledge or such a system. I hope this clarifies the “still considered a theory” part. Yes, general relativity is (still) considered a theory, and it will remain a theory, but not because it lacks plenty of experimental and observational proof. In fact, when the theory was born, Einstein himself proposed “three classical tests” of general relativity: In addition to these three classical tests, Shapiro in the 1960s proposed a fourth: rays of light or, for that matter, radio waves, passing near a massive object like the Sun, would suffer a delay that is the combined effect of the light rays following a slightly curved path and also slowed down (as measured by us, distant observers in our reference frame) due to gravitational time dilation. This Shapiro delay has been confirmed numerous times using spacecraft, and has been used ever since the 1960s as a routine part of precision radio-navigation software codes navigating spacecraft in the solar system. Since then, we have had many more confirmations of the effects of general relativity. Folks often mention the GPS constellation, which of course would not work at the desired precision if we didn’t account for general relativistic correction. There have also been other experiments involving, e.g., clocks in orbiting spacecraft. Coming up to the present day, high-accuracy atomic clocks are sensitive enough to detect changes in the gravitational field due to a few ten centimeters or less of a change in altitude. Take two such clocks, one on the floor, one on a laboratory bench and right there, you can measure a key prediction of general relativity, gravitational time dilation. So the general theory of relativity represents well-established science, with robust experimental evidence supporting its predictions here in the solar system and in laboratory environments. Whether or not the theory will survive cosmological tests remains a bit of an open question: our persistent failure to detect dark matter and dark energy directly in numerous experiments probing different hypotheses for their existence, along with the existing issues that affect the standard cosmological model leave the door ever so slightly open to modified theories of gravitation that would predict deviations from Einstein’s theory on galactic and extragalactic scales. Can you explain the calculation for determining the time it takes for an object to fall into a black hole while traveling at the speed of light? First of all, you have to disabuse yourself of the notion that an object is traveling at a speed of… whatever. Speed is not an inherent property. The theory of relativity is called relativity for a reason: Speed is always relative. It is a relationship between two reference frames. So let us look at an hapless traveler falling into a black hole. What is that traveler’s speed? Well, as I just said, it is meaningless to speak of that traveler’s speed as an inherent property. The traveler’s speed depends on who is looking. OK, so we are looking. From some safe position outside the black hole’s event horizon. What do we see? Why, we see the traveler approach the place where the horizon will presumably form. Except that, the closer he gets to that place, the slower he appears to us, due to extreme gravitational time dilation. In fact, we literally (and I mean literally, not some figure-of-speech) never get to see the traveler actually reach the horizon. That moment — indeed, the moment when the horizon forms in the first place — remains for us forever in the future, due to extreme, runaway gravitational time dilation. And this is where we have a paradoxical situation. We know that the traveler reaches the vacuum speed of light at the horizon; that’s how black holes work. But from our perspective, the traveler’s speed actually drops to zero because of extreme gravitational time dilation! Well, guess what: in our reference frame, the speed of anything, including light itself, drops to zero at the horizon. Except that “the horizon” is not a place here and now, but a moment in time in our infinite future: Which is to say, we will see things slow down, slow down exponentially, but the moment when the horizon forms, the moment when all those speeds reach zero in our reference frame, will forever remain in our future. In fact, in our reference frame there is no meaningful way to describe the horizon or what’s “inside”. That’s why the darn thing is actually called a “horizon”! OK, what about the traveler’s perspective, then? Well, apart from increasing tides, he’d experience nothing special if he’s not looking out through the portholes of his spaceship. If the black hole is very, very large, tidal forces won’t be excessive even as he approaches, and crosses, the horizon. But he is doomed: he is now in a mini-universe that is collapsing around him, with no means of escape unless he has a time machine, because for him, the horizon has now become a moment of time in the past, and the only way to escape, to cross the horizon backwards, is by traveling into the past. In due course his mini-universe collapses and the world ends. The calculations are not elementary but not particularly hard either. The key equation is the so-called geodesic equation that describes freefalling trajectories. To model things from the traveler’s perspective, we need a coordinate system that covers both the interior and the exterior of the event horizon; one such coordinate system is called Kruskal—Szekeres coordinates. Whatever coordinate system we pick, we can calculate the “proper time”, i.e., the amount of time the traveler would measure, to reach the event horizon of the black hole and to reach the singularity (i.e., the “end of the world” for the mini-universe enclosed by the horizon.) Lastly, I hasten to add that this is classical relativity. Once we introduce quantum physics, things change, since black holes evaporate in finite time, so the traveler may never experience the horizon in the first place. But that’s a different story. Debroglie says wavelength is inversely proportional to velocity. But velocity is relative, and it is 0 in that particle’s resting frame of reference. So what does it mean for a particle to have infinite wavelength? Well, if you think of the de Broglie wavelength as a means to characterize how a particle moves, in the reference frame in which the particle is at rest, infinite wavelength (zero frequency) simply means that the particle is not moving. I know, it sounds kind of tautological, but that’s what it boils down to: no movement, no wave, zero frequency, hence infinite wavelength. Of course keep in mind that we’re not talking about a physical wave here. The wavelength here is simply a mathematical characterization of the amplitude of the particle’s wavefunction, which determines the probability density of finding the particle in a given state. Zero momentum means that the particle is not moving, but it can be with equal probability anywhere. This also follows from the uncertainty principle, since precise determination of a particle’s momentum means its position is completely indeterminate. Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? Absolutely. In the context of cosmological physics, matter and antimatter are both “ordinary”, visible matter, made up of particles that interact with each other and with the electromagnetic field. Dark matter does not interact with the electromagnetic field (or if it does, it does so very, very, very weakly) and does not interact with normal matter (which includes antimatter). We don’t know what dark matter is (we cannot even be sure that it exists) but if there is such a thing, this is its defining characteristic. In contrast, antimatter very much interacts with normal matter. So much so, that this is how we know that even distant regions of the visible universe are dominated by normal matter, not antimatter. How do we know? Matter is everywhere, there are hydrogen atoms even in intergalactic space. If there were, e.g., distant galaxy clusters made of antimatter, the boundary region between antimatter and normal matter regions would “glow” in the gamma ray part of the spectrum from the occasional matter-antimatter interactions. Granted, in the very low density intergalactic medium, such collisions would be infrequent, but on the other hand, the volumes are ginormous, and the resulting gamma ray background would be observable.

Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves have both energy and momentum. When an object emits some light in a specific direction, it is pushed backwards ever so slightly. Similarly, when an object absorbs or reflects light, it is pushed by that light. (Experimental spacecraft with solar sails use the momentum of sunlight to accelerate.) As to sound waves, you can even visualize it. A sound wave is a pressure wave. Recall what happens when a very loud sound wave hits, say, a window pane. The glass shatters. It shatters because of the force (change in momentum) as momentum from the incoming sound wave is transferred to the glass. So yes, sound waves also carry momentum. As do waves in general. Here, I just stumbled upon this article by a Charles S. Peskin that tells you everything you need to know about the momentum of waves. For a second, I thought it was the Peskin of "Peskin and Schroeder" fame, i.e., one of the authors of perhaps the best current textbook on quantum field theory, but no, that's another Pesking, Michael E. Even so, this write-up on wave momenta is good. Yes there's math but I think also enough explanation for it to make sense even if you skip over most of the equations. Why is light a particle and a wave at the same time? Can you explain the two slot experiment? “Wave-particle duality” is another one of those unfortunate phrases that are invented to help explain a difficult concept, but do more harm than good in the end. So here is the thing when it comes to quantum phenomena: the exact outcome of a measurement, carried out using a classical instrument (say, the human eyeball) cannot be predicted. We can only predict probabilities. But it’s not like “classical” probabilities. The limitation does not arise from the fact that we lack full knowledge of the system. Rather, the exact outcome of an experiment does not exist until, well, until it exists. It is not some technological limitation: it is not predictable in principle. But then… what can we predict? We can predict probabilities. And these probabilities are governed by an equation that, for all practical intents and purposes, travel like a wave. Waves that interfere with one another. Waves that reinforce or cancel one another at various places. In the end, though we do not observe these waves. We observe, say, the impact of a photon. There! A particle, making its appearance at a specific place, say, a specific point on your retina when you see a brief flash of light. But “en route”, there was no particle. We cannot identify the path that the particle traveled in order to reach its destination because no such path exists. What we can do is explore that “probability wave” as it “travels” from source to destination. This allows us to assign specific probabilities as to where the “particle” might be observed when it comes to that. So you see… that thing we observe is really not a particle: a particle, like a miniature cannonball, would follow a well-defined trajectory, and in this case, no such trajectory exists. But that thing we observe is really not a wave either. The “wave” in question is a mathematical abstraction, a probability amplitude, not a “thing”. The “thing” is the impact of the photon on your retina, which is particle-like behavior, but again, a true particle would have a path associated with it. And it is this point that I need to offer a reminder that, like it or not, quantum physics cannot be intuited. It is outside the ability of the human mind to intuit these things, just as, say, a language model like GPT cannot “intuit” an image or a sound, as it lacks the ability to process images or sounds. It can still reason about them, but that reasoning requires discipline and, well, knowledge of mathematics. We are in the same shoes here: With our scientific discipline and mathematical tools, we can make robust predictions about the quantum world. But we make these predictions precisely because we let go of our desire to intuit the quantum world and instead, chose to follow the math (verified by experiment, of course). So that’s my advice: Do not take this “wave-particle” business literally, as an invitation to try to intuit the unintuitable. Or if you must, at least remind yourself that the “wave” is a probability wave (not a physical thing), and the “particle” is not really a particle with a definite path, even if in the end, when we observe it (but only then!) it may masquerade as one. What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Oh my, this is a hard question to answer... at least in a form suitable for a Quora answer. Let me try to keep it as simple as possible, which means necessarily skipping over some details, but still. You know what vectors are, right? Basically, quantities that have a magnitude and a direction. You may have learned to form inner products of vectors, but that's a misleading notion on its own right. The inner product is formed between a vector and a "covector". One way to think about it, perhaps, is that whereas a vector may be measuring a length and a direction, a covector is measuring the change of something along that length. So whereas vectors are measured using, say, meters or feet, covectors are measured using "inverse" units of length, i.e., meters or feet are now in the denominator. So say, a vector measures a length in a certain direction as 1 meter. Or 100 centimeters. Someone says that they have distributed marbles with a density of 10 marbles per meter. Or 0.1 marbles per centimeter. So now you form an inner product... between a 1-meter vector and the marble density of 10 marbles per meter. Multiply the two, and you get 10 marbles. Change the coordinate system from meters to centimeters: Now you have a 100-cm vector and 0.1 marbles per cm. Multiply the two and... again you get 10 marbles! The inner product between a vector and a covector yields a "scalar", a pure number that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. This is important. So then, we can actually "define" a covector as the thing that maps a vector into a scalar by applying the inner product. What do you call a thing that maps not one but two vectors into a scalar? Wait, two vectors? Why would we want to do that? Well, how about characterizing how a force works on a surface. The force is a vector. The surface, a small surface element that is, can be characterized by a vector: its "normal" vector indicating its orientation and size. In continuum mechanics, we look at surface elements and the force acting on them. That force can be present due to pressure and stresses in the material. The point is, we need to relate these two vectors together... and the relationship is accomplished by introducing a thing called the "stress tensor", which can basically form an inner product with this pair of vectors. This also happens to be one of the earliest (early 19th century!) applications of tensors in physics. And this then allows us to generalize. If a covector maps a vector into a scalar, a covariant rank-N tensor can map N vectors into a scalar. Conversely, a vector can map a covector into a scalar; so a contravariant rank-N tensor can map N covectors into a scalar. And it is then easy to form "mixed index" tensors that map a collection of, say, N vectors and K covectors into a scalar. That's what tensors do: establish a relationship between vectors and covectors, mapping them into scalar quantities that do not depend on the choice of coordinate system in which the vectors are measured or expressed. Rank-2 tensors can be easily represented using matrices (though technically, it's only the rank-2 mixed index tensors, which map one vector and one covector into a scalar, that should be written as such, rows corresponding to the covariant, columns to the contravariant features of the tensor.) Higher-rank tensors are not that easy to represent as they require either multiple matrices or higher-domensional (cubic, etc.) structures which are not easy to put on paper. One of the wonderful things about tensors, however, is that they allow us to talk about physics without picking a specific coordinate system! If a vector V and a covector U form a scalar, say, V ⋅ U = 1 , that equation remains valid regardless of the coordinate system chosen. This allows us to distinguish physics (the actual things) from mathematics (the representation of those things) very cleanly. Going back to the inner product, we can of course calculate the inner product between two vectors if we have a corresponding rank-2 covariant tensor that we use to map the pair of vectors into a number. The "metric tensor" does this. The number, in this case, may be the length of the small difference between two near-identical vectors. This turns out to be an effective measure of the intrinsic geometry of the plane, of space, of spacetime. Normally, this "metric tensor" is just a generalization of the Pythagorean rule to calculate distances. But things get more complicated in general relativity, where the geometry of spacetime varies from place to place. So say, take a vector. Displace it so that it moves a tiny distance away, following a closed path, arriving back at its point of origin. So now you have a second vector (the direction of the displacement); a third vector (the direction the displaced vector follows when it arrives back at the point of origin); and a fourth vector (the final vector after arrival). The first and the fourth vector would be identical in Euclidean space. They are not in general relativity. The rank-4 tensor that relates these four vectors is the "Riemann curvature tensor", its value changing from point to point reflecting changing curvature. The relationship between this curvature tensor and the presence of matter amounts to the fundamental statement of general relativity, in the form of Einstein's field equations. Well, that's the gist of it. As I said, I glossed over many details. But hopefully at least it's a meaningful glimpse of the role of tensors in physics, relativity theory in particular. Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Let me describe to you an imaginary journey into a classical black hole. ("Classical" in the sense that I am ignoring quantum effects, notably Hawking radiation, which might even prevent the black hole from forming in the first place. So let's say that you are not only in a very good spaceship, but you are also almost imprevious to extreme acceleration and extreme tidal forces. You hope into your spaceship, travel to the nearest collapsing sphere of matter that will ultimately form a black hole, and choose a trajectory that will end up in the black hole as well. If the collapsing matter has negligible pressure, its collapse will not be slowed down by any means. Yet to those on the outside, the process of the collapse will appear to slow as the cloud gets close to becoming a black hole. That is because of extreme gravitational time dilation: anything that happens near this collapsing cloud of matter will appear in slow motion to anyone far away. Not to you though. You will find that you will approach the surface of this collapsing cloud, but you won't quite be able to catch up with it. Meanwhile, however, as the gravitational field gets stronger, you will notice that what was a spherical surface below now appears to "curl up" on the sides. That is because of the gravitational deflection of light: many light rays that start off going upward will be bent downward, so they will appear to hit your eyeball from above! What was one a surface below begins to form a wall around you, and soon enough, it will feel like you are in a vertical tunnel, or well, its opening rapidly closing above you. Suppose you chicken out at the very last split second, punch a button, and with your Extremely Powerful Rocket [tm] you escape. Much to your surprise, you'll find that what has taken only a few seconds by your reckoning took a year outside. Or a thousand years. Or a quintillion years. This is why those on the outside can never be sure that the black hole even forms; no matter how long they wait, there's a chance that you re-emerge. It's only a question of how close you cut it before punching out. But what if you don't? Well, there will be a moment when the matter above your head closes up. There is no opening anymore. No walls really, either, as this is also the moment when you caught up with all the collapsing matter after all, so now you are inside the cloud. Inside a homogeneous (same everywhere) isotropic (no preferred direction) cloud of matter that forms a collapsing mini-universe, in which you are trapped. The moment when this happened is the event horizon. NOT a place. Not a location to which you can return. A moment — now a moment in the past — of time. So without a time machine, you are doomed. This mini-universe is a collapsing universe, the exact opposite of the kind of universe we seem to live in, outside of the black hole. Second by second, minute by minute it becomes denser. (Or millisecond by millisecond, if the collapsing cloud weighed "only" as much as, say, three times the mass of our Sun, or a million times the mass of the Earth.) Did I say same everywhere? Yes, I did. I meant it. There is no center, no edge of this cloud. This entire self-enclosed mini-universe is filled with matter everywhere. And you have very little time left. And perhaps that's when you recall something that you may have heard before in the past: The so-called "singularity" is not some center either. Rather, it is the moment in time when density, pressure, temperature, etc., everything in this mini-universe diverges, becomes infinite. The mini-universe ceases to exist (it's called geodesic incompleteness). Along with you, of course. Think this scenario through and now contemplate if it is even meaningful to talk about "destroying" a black hole. What exactly would that "destruction" do? Remember, to those on the outside, the black hole does not even exist yet, no matter how long they wait. Whereas for those on the inside, the black hole is the ONLY thing that exists, and its fate is sealed: soon enough everything, including time itself (!) comes to an end in this doomed mini-universe.

Einstein believed quantum mechanics wasn’t fundamental and there must be a deeper theory. Was he correct? Well… yes and no, but context is all-important here. Einstein passed away in 1955. At the time, modern quantum field theory was still in its infancy. Yang-Mills theory that proved fundamental to the development of the Standard Model was just a few months old. In any case, I doubt Einstein had more than a very superficial familiarity with then-recent developments. The quantum mechanics that he was familiar with was basically quantum particle theory, characterized by the Schrödinger equation or maybe the relativistic Dirac equation, which were predominantly interpreted in accordance with the Copenhagen school as equations that yield a probability amplitude. Quite clearly, Einstein was not comfortable with physics that yielded only probabilities. Moreover, the Copenhagen interpretation assigns a role to the “observer”, which is fundamentally at odds with a world view in which Nature does what it does, regardless of whether it is observed or not by a human, a cat, or some instrument. So what do we know that Einstein didn’t? For starters, modern quantum field theory and the Standard Model of particle physics. Then there’s also Bell’s theorem that demonstrates that quantum physics is essentially nonlocal, which is to say, the behavior of the system is governed, in part, by constraints that cannot be nailed down to any specific location in space or moment in time. What it means, in practice, is that the state of a quantum system is constrained not just by the past and the present but also by the future, yet the physics remains causal in the sense that rearranging something in the future has no observable consequences on the past (sorry, no quantum time machines). In light of this, the probabilistic interpretation gains a new meaning: ignore the future constraint and the system becomes underdetermined. Instead of telling us what the future will be, the (underdetermined) wavefunction now indeed just yields probabilities. When the future becomes the present, and the outcome of an experiment becomes known, the probability becomes a certainty and we can replace the old wavefunction with a new one (“wavefunction collapse”) in our description of the system. Would this have made Einstein more comfortable? I don’t know. But I do believe that this is markedly different from the quantum physics Einstein knew. Which implies that yes, he was right to criticize quantum mechanics and, in particular, its Copenhagen interpretation. As a local theory, quantum mechanics is necessarily incomplete (again, I am alluding to Bell’s theorem here) and leads to the unsatisfying probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. But what we got in exchange is, in some ways, even weirder. Yes, quantum field theory has spectacular successes. It can do what quantum mechanics could not ever do, model how particles are created and destroyed. It is also robustly causal and relativistic. But it is just as nonlocal as quantum physics has ever been, and with Bell’s theorem, we know that this nonlocality is not going to go away. Then there’s the problem of renormalizability: We have no renormalizable quantum field theory of gravitation. To many, it seems to imply that the Standard Model (and by extension, quantum field theory as a whole) is just a useful “effective” theory, which will fail at the Planck energy scale, to be replaced by something more fundamental that would unify particle physics with gravity in a more satisfactory way than, say, semiclassical gravity. But much of what I described here happened after Einstein’s death. The quantum theory that he was critical of was really not modern quantum field theory, but quantum particle physics, along with the probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. I think his criticism of that school of thought was spot on. What was not spot on is his relentless attempt to construct a more fundamental classical theory, which consumed much of his time in the final decades of his life, but ultimately proved futile, little more than a half-forgotten footnote in the history of modern physics. (To anyone seriously interested in the subject, beyond the superb scientific biography of Einstein by Abraham Pais, I’d recommend the hard-to-find 1966 monograph, Einstein’s Unified Field Theory, by Marie-Antoinette Tonnelat.) Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity? I think it was a bit more nuanced than that. Einstein and Hilbert corresponded frequently in 1915, as they were both working on the problem of finding the field equations of gravitation. Einstein was trying to discover the field equations more or less heuristically. He was not concerned with the nature of matter. He left the stress-energy tensor essentially unconstrained other than its basic symmetry properties. His theory was a theory of gravitation, not matter. Hilbert, on the other hand, inspired in part by earlier work by Mie, was more specific. His stress-energy tensor was intended to be representative of what we today would call a classical "theory of everything", encompassing electromagnetic fields and matter. The two corrresponding frequently in November 1915. Based on what we know (see, e.g., Abraham Pais's scientific biography of Einstein), I think it is fair to say that the physical theory of general relativity is undeniably Einstein's (Hilbert himself referred to this as Einstein's theory.) It seems likely that they both discovered the field equations independently, though undoubtedly, they both benefited from their frequent correspondence. Hilbert deserves credit for showing us the way to derive the field equations of gravitation from an action principle, as opposed to just postulating them like Einstein did. It should be stressed perhaps that by late 1915, the goal was in sight and the nature of the theory that Einstein sought was clearly understood. The missing bit? It seemed clear that the gravitational field is represented by the contracted Riemann curvature tensor, i.e., the Ricci-tensor R μ ν . However, the Ricci tensor does not have the symmetry properties associated with the stress-energy tensor of matter, which is to say, the Ricci-tensor is not divergence-free. The key final step in formulating the field equations is the inclusion of the − 1 2 R g μ ν term in the field equations. This term would follow from Hilbert's action, but based on, e.g., surviving galley proofs, it appears that this final form was not yet present in Hilbert's initial draft, only in later (1916) revisions. (See also General relativity priority dispute - Wikipedia for some details.) Hilbert's "mistake" if it can be called that is that he was perhaps too ambitious: Using Mie's work, he was trying to construct "the foundations of physics" (the explicit title of his paper). In contrast, Einstein was focusing on "the field equations of gravitation" (that was the actual title he used). Hilbert's original approach, as explained by Pais, also contained mistakes not related to the specific form of the field equations. Further, Pais suggests (and he’s probably right) that although the two men corresponded frequently, they pursued very different approaches and different goals, and may have “talked past each other”, neither paying sufficient attention to absorb the approach of the other. Today, we call the tensor G μ ν = R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν the Einstein tensor; the field equations of gravitation are the Einstein equations; however, the action integral from which these field equations can be derived, S = ∫ d 4 x √ − g ( 1 2 κ R + L m a t t e r ) is called the Einstein-Hilbert action. Einstein and Hilbert had a bit of a dispute but their later correspondence remains friendly. The reason for the dispute probably had nothing to do with the actual discoveries in late November 1915, and may have had something to do with Einstein feeling that Hilbert plagiarized some ideas he presented in a talk (again, according to Pais). Everywhere we are surrounded by a lot of visible electromagnetic waves. Why don’t we see a lots of black patterns of destructive interactions of light waves? Actually, you see them all the time. Take a light source, preferably something that has a narrow beam of light. Aim it at a wall. You see a spot of light. Everywhere else on the wall, you see no light. (None from that source anyway.) Now take the wave equations that govern that light as it is emitted by the source and travels through space to arrive at the wall. That wave equation does not vanish outside the light beam. It’s there, everywhere. However, there is no significant constructive interference outside the projected spot of light. Destructive interference prevails. The wall remains dark. How do I know? Say, I wish to solve the wave equations in this case to arrive at a robust, wave-theoretical solution of the projection. Again, the waves are there, everywhere, characterized by a messy integral expression in the mathematical model. That integral usually does not have a neat, clean solution. Rather, I am forced to utilize sensible approximations, for instance the so-called method of stationary phase. The method of stationary phase explicitly picks the light path that corresponds to the strong constructive interference between waves, and discards those paths that are characterized by destructive interference. The result is the calculated spot on the wall. I.e., the method yields the light path that I would calculate using geometric optics, as it tells me precisely where the spot of light will appear. Going beyond either geometric optics or the method of stationary phase, more sophisticated numerical methods might reveal something more than a single spot; the spot may be surrounded by concentric rings of light or similar artifacts, rapidly diminishing in brightness. Here, I have an actual example from work I’ve done in the past. Although this one depicts a case of gravitational lensing, the principles are the same: The image on the left shows an “Einstein cross” (four spots of light) due to a particular (slightly off-axis) gravitational lens, calculated using the method of stationary phase, i.e., geometric optics basically. The image on the right shows the exact same thing, but a more sophisticated numerical integration reveals that there is also light between the spots. In any case, the key message should be clear. The very fact that, despite the fundamental wave nature of light, we see the result of geometric optics everywhere — rays of light, spots of light, shadows, etc., indeed the very fact that our eyes work and can form sharp images — is a result of the combined effects of constructive and destructive interference. In these two images, too, light is everywhere; it’s just that in places where the image appears black, destructive interference won the game. Is the range of gravitational force infinite, diminishing toward but never reaching zero? None of the fundamental (or even not-so-fundamental) forces disappear, but the manner in which they diminish differs. Gravitation and electromagnetism are said to have “infinite” range, because the potential decreases “only” as the inverse of distance, and consequently, the force, which is to say, the gradient (rate of steepest change) diminishes as the inverse square of distance. So it still becomes rather tiny at a great distance from the source, but it’s still there. In contrast, forces mediated by massive particles in the quantum picture are said to have a “finite” range. Near the source, these forces behave just like gravity or electromagnetism. But when you reach a characteristic distance (which is proportional to the inverse of the mass of the force carrier particle) the potential, hence the force, begins to drop very rapidly, exponentially as a matter of fact. Examples fot this include the “weak” force (not really that weak, but it has a very finite range as the force carrier particles, the W and Z-bosons, are very massive), and also the “residual strong force”, aka. the “nuclear force” that is responsible for holding protons and neutrons together inside atoms. As to what the nuclear force is a residual of, whoa, things get really interesting there! The strong force, which holds quarks together, actually increases with distance! When the quarks are very close together, there’s barely any force. The quarks behave like free particles, or almost (this is called asymptotic freedom). But start pulling them apart and the force stiffens. You might think that this implies infinite range, but it really doesn’t; rather, when you pump enough energy into the system pulling two quarks apart, that energy is converted into a new quark-antiquark pair, and the bond “snaps”. Kind of like pulling a string: as you pull, eventually the string breaks, and you end up with two strings, with new endpoints. Ultimately of course all these pretty pictorial representations are just approximations; what we are really describing is a multitude of interacting quantum fields and their excited states. The “virtual particles” that may be used to describe them have no physical reality whatsoever; rather, they are convenient mathematical bookkeeping devices as we keep track of terms in a mathematical expression (a perturbative expansion). Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it? I presume this question is about quantum mechanics. In the classical world, we’re used to things working, well, normally. Take a flying cannonball. At any given moment in time, we can describe its position x and we can describe its velocity, or rather, its momentum p (same thing as velocity, for all practical intents and purposes.) The quantities x and p are numbers (maybe sets of numbers, i.e., coordinates or coordinate components, but expressed using numbers nonetheless.) Because they are numbers, we can multiply them in any order: the products p ⋅ x and x ⋅ p represent the same thing. This all makes perfectly good sense, but Nature has this nasty habit of not obeying our expectations when it comes to what we think makes good sense and what does not. As it turns out, things in Nature do not obey this simple arithmetic. Particles are not acting like miniature cannonballs. They do not have positions and momenta. They have states. And to the extent that they exhibit properties that can be interpreted, viewed, measured as positions or momenta under the right circumstances, these can be represented in mathematics by so-called operators like ^ x or ^ p , acting on a state ψ . And these operators do not obey the (commutative) rule of multiplication: ^ p ⋅ ^ x ≠ ^ x ⋅ ^ p . This is the essence of quantum physics. And this has two consequences. First, that state of the quantum system, ψ . It is governed by the famous Schrödinger equation. That equation is a “wave equation”, which is to say, under most circumstances it will give some kind of a periodic solution. So the state of this quantum system will have wave-like behavior, which includes, e.g., constructive and destructive interference, something cannonballs never do. Second, those operators I mentioned, for positions and momenta: Under the right circumstances they yield measurable numbers. So with the right experiment, that quantum system still exhibits behavior that makes it appear like a miniature cannonball. So when you fire, say, an electron, while the electron is en route it does not have a position of a momentum in the classical sense. Its existence is described by the state ψ , its wavefunction. But when it impacts, say, the fluorescent screen of a CRT, that interaction confines it to a well-defined position. Its position operator ^ x , acting on its state, produces a set of coordinates, the location where you see a flash on the screen. If this explanation appears a little abstract, a little hard to make sense of, that is no accident. Quantum physics cannot be intuited. To use a stupid analogy, almost all of us had a chance to play with language models like ChatGPT in the past year or so. Ignoring their more recent attempts to integrate language and visual capabilities, the original language model has no visual experiences. No ability to intuit or visualize anything related to space or geometry. It can still reason about these things, but often it struggles, as its words are not connected to any experience that it would have at its disposal. We humans are in the same situation with quantum physics. Just as language models have no visual cortex, our brains lack a “quantum physics cortex” that would allow us to intuit the quantum world. Therefore, like the language models, we have to resort to painful, slow, step-by-step reasoning, relying on the reasonably precise language of mathematics. However painful this feels, it is important to remember that any attempt to visualize quantum physics using our intuition that is rooted in classical physics is not only doomed to fail, it will likely become an obstacle to understanding. Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them. What are the challenges and potential designs for a SpaceX Interstellar probe using miniaturized black hole propulsion, theorized to harness Hawking radiation as thrust? First of all, the only (ONLY!) known mechanism to produce a black hole is stellar collapse. For that, you need at the very least three times the mass of the Sun, which is a million times the mass of the Earth. The lifetime of that black hole is about 3.13 × 10 68 years, and at present, its Hawking radiation output is 10 − 29 watts. But let us suppose that some magic (not physics) allows us to create a “miniaturized” black hole. How miniaturized? Say, 1 metric ton? Do different colors and wavelengths of light have different speeds when traveling through space-time? No, they do not, and this is indeed a very important property of light. The speed of a light ray in the vacuum does not depend on its energy or frequency (i.e., its color). All light rays follow the same “null geodesics” of spacetime, as determined by the gravitational field. This would not be the case if the particles that mediate electromagnetism, photons, were massive. In that case, the photon’s speed would depend on its energy. In a gravitational field, light rays of different color would follow different trajectories. When light rays are deflected by a massive body, such as the Sun, different colors would be deflected by a different angle. We’d see white light split into the colors of the rainbow. We do not see this with gravitational lensing. Not with the Sun, not with distant astrophysical lenses. In fact, gravitational lensing observations are one of the means by which we can establish experimental limits on the maximum mass that photons could have without us noticing. (There are other methods, some even more sensitive.) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it? White holes are theoretical constructs, time-reversed versions of the Schwarzschild (or Kerr) solutions of general relativity. Take the words, “time-reversed”, very seriously. The Schwarzschild solution is not about the object that is the source of gravitation. It is about the gravitational field everywhere surrounding that object, all the way to infinity. In other words, the entire cosmos. So when we say “time reversed”, we are talking about a time-reversed cosmos. Hawking radiation is predicted based on an analysis that places quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of a gravitating object. Contrary to popularizations, the radiation arises not because of the presence of an event horizon (which, in the case of black holes, remains forever in any outside observer’s future) but because of a past-future asymmetry in an object in a state of perpetual collapse. Now reverse time and see what you get! Incoming radiation. That’s what a white hole does. It absorbs Hawking radiation due to its gravitational vacuum polarization. How can that be? Again, take time-reversed very seriously. Think about this for a moment. You can’t fall into a white hole, right? But wait… a white hole still has attractive gravity! Time-reversed means that something orbiting a white hole would be going backwards compared to what you might see under identical circumstances near a black hole, but when you go backwards around a circle, it’s still a circle. So why can you not fall into a white hole? Because you are not in the white hole in the future. Again, time-reversed. It means causality is thrown out the window, and the future determines the past or the present. Compared to that, the idea that the white hole’s gravitational vacuum polarization somehow causes the rest of the universe to contribute to its “negative” Hawking radiation almost sounds quaint. Oh, did I say that white hole are theoretical constructs? Let me stress that again. Mathematical games, not observed physics. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the origin of the energy resulting in an explosion during the merger of two neutron stars that do not result in a black hole? Black hole, no black hole, the energy is there, the end result doesn’t matter much. At first it is gravitational potential energy: the “ability to do work”, i.e., bring things into motion. When the two stars are far apart but attracted to each other, as they get closer, they speed up. So potential energy “does work”, gets converted into kinetic energy. A good chunk of that kinetic energy is radiated away in the form of gravitational radiation as the two stars orbit each other in an ever tighter inspiral, reaching a substantial fraction of the vacuum speed of light towards the end. But then, kaboom, they collide. That means that whatever kinetic energy they have left (which is to say, stupendous amounts of kinetic energy when an entire star moves at a sizable percentage of the speed of light) is now converted into heat. Think of a large meteorite impact… and now multiply that by, I don’t know, maybe a 30-digit number. So if the end product is not a black hole, what we have instead is an object that is heated to insane high temperatures as a result. (This also becomes a factory for heavy elements. Chances are your own body contains quite a few atoms that were produced in such a collision.) As a matter of fact, more energy is released by the impact if the end result is not a black hole, as all that heat can radiate away, instead of being gobbled up by the resulting black hole. But in the end, it’s just plain old gravitational potential energy, converted into motion (kinetic energy) and, upon impact, into more random motion (heat). Nothing fancy, really, apart from the sizes and scales involved. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Was Heisenberg the first one to promote the use of tensors in physics? No, it was not Heisenberg. Let me show you a snapshot from a page from an interesting paper: Sure, the notation is a bit archaic, but what you are looking at is the Cauchy stress tensor, which characterizes the stresses and pressures in a medium. This snapshot is from a later reprint of Cauchy’s 1827 paper, De la pression ou tension dans un corps solide [Ex. Math. 2 (1827) p. 42]. So as you can see, tensors were already in use in mathematical physics two centuries ago. Later, in the early 20th century, tensors became the essential tool for relativity theory, especially general relativity. The reason is that the tensor concept perfectly captures the difference between the geometric object (which exists independently of any choice of coordinates) vs. its representation in a specific coordinate system. The independence of physics from the coordinates used to represent it is a fundamental concept in relativity theory (and, well, modern physics in general). Heisenberg, incidentally, did not use tensors much to my knowledge. His matrix mechanics was something else: it was a means to represent the observables of quantum physics, for instance, positions and momenta that do not behave like the ordinary numbers of classical physics, specifically they do not commute under multiplication. Later it was shown that Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics was mathematically equivalent to representing the same quantities using function operators acting on Schrödinger’s wavefunction. But those matrices were not used to represent tensor quantities. However, tensors entered the world of quantum physics with a vengeance, starting with the 1930s, with the development of quantum field theory. What happens to matter when it falls into a black hole? Is it destroyed or stored as energy? Can you provide an explanation for this phenomenon? The problem with questions like this can be summed up with that one word used in the question itself: “when”. You see, a black hole is not just some physical object that exists here and now. We are talking relativity theory here, after all, extreme relativity, with both space and time involved. How much time? Well, that’s the tricky part. The closer something gets to a black hole, the stronger the gravitational field in its vicinity. And a strong gravitational field means time dilation. Not just minute time dilation, mind you, like here on the surface of the Earth, where clocks one part in a billion, give or take, slower compared to clocks in deep space. Extreme time dilation. Long story short, concerning that “when”: The question as to when an object falls into a black hole is answered, for us outside observers, by a simple word: never. That is to say, near the black hole’s event horizon, time dilation becomes divergent. Infinite. The moment when an infalling object would reach the event horizon remains forever in the future for outside observers. What about infalling observers? Well, they’d find themselves in a collapsing mini-universe, consisting of all things that ever fell, ever will fall into the black hole. This universe has a (very) finite lifespan. The famed singularity? That’s not some place you can avoid. It’s the future moment in time when this mini-universe comes to an end. But for outside observers, that never happens. Stuff falling into a black hole never reaches that black hole. In fact, this is precisely why black holes, in some of the older or foreign literature, were often called “frozen stars”. So in a very real sense, all that matter is still there, in the process of falling. Invisible to us due to the same time dilation that causes extreme redshift, so any signal from infalling matter is shifted into oblivion. So the black hole, for all intents and purposes, appears “black” (that is, not visible) but we know, assuming that our math is correct, that it represents a state of continued collapse (the title of the famous 1939 Oppenheimer-Snyder paper, which first described such collapse, reflects this: On Continued Gravitational Contraction.) **Question for a physicist: ** How are stars born according to the general theory of relativity? The general theory of relativity has very little to do with it, since stellar birth does not involve gravitational fields that come even close to being relativistic. So insofar as stellar births are concerned, Newtonian gravity will do just fine. The basic idea is this: When you have a cloud of stuff with minor density fluctuations, under the influence of gravity those fluctuations tend to grow over time. Where matter was denser to begin with, there’s more gravity, attracting more matter. Where matter was less dense to begin with, there’s less gravity and slower attraction. When the stuff is normal matter, say, mostly hydrogen, however, atoms and molecules eventually begin to collide. The infall becomes more randomized, kinetic energy turning into heat as atoms and molecules bounce off each other. It also means rising pressure, which will slow down the density growth. And that loss of kinetic energy to heat, which is radiated away? It means that stuff, once together, sticks together, having lost some or all of its kinetic energy that’d be needed for it to fly apart again. Continue the process for a while, and deep in the interior of the hydrogen cloud eventually the pressure and temperature become high enough for fusion. That is to say, hydrogen atoms will collide often enough, and powerfully enough, to occasionally fuse together. When that happens, a lot of energy is released in the form of high-speed particles like gamma ray photons, which then bounce into other things, transferring their kinetic energy, heating things up. Ultimately that heat escapes the cloud; viewed from the outside, the cloud begins to warm up, begins the glow, even as it continues to contract. Eventually, it settles down to an equilibrium between gravity and pressure. Meanwhile, its glow, its radiation, helps sweep away some of the leftover gas that did coalesce with the rest. What you’re left with is a fairly dense ball of gas, in the interior of which now nuclear fusion takes place at a steady rate. Not very fast, mind you; if the mass of the cloud is that of our Sun, chances are it’s producing no more heat per unit volume than a well-maintained compost pile. Except that it can continue doing that for billions of years. And that’s how a star is born. General relativity? The role it plays is minuscule, a tiny, tiny modification of Newtonian gravity. A few parts in a million, tops. Mind you, if that star is heavier, eventually it might collapse into an object with gravity so strong, general relativity can no longer be ignored, rather, it plays a major role. That would be a neutron star. However, that state comes at the end, not the beginning, of a star’s life cycle. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Planck length is the smallest measurable length, and the scale at which we require new laws of quantum gravity. If we defined laws of quantum gravity, allowing us to predict interaction at these lengths, could we measure these lengths? Cite papers! First of all, no, the Planck length is not the smallest measurable length. If by “measurable”, we mean practically measurable, the smallest measurable length is many orders of magnitude greater. If by “measurable” we mean measurable in principle, I can easily envision an interference experiment in deep space, using high frequency gamma rays and instrumentation on the solar system’s scale, that can measure differences in wavelength smaller than the Planck length. Concerning quantum gravity, I think a more accurate statement is that if gravity is indeed a quantum theory (keep in mind, there are theoretical proposals out there in which gravity remains fundamentally classical) then yes, we expect its quantum nature to manifest itself at the Planck scale. However, even if I assume that we do find a convincing quantum theory of gravitation and it receives some experimental confirmation, it still does not mean that we’d be able in practice to measure lengths at the Planck scale. Cite papers? Cannot really think of any… except perhaps Freeman Dyson’s Poincaré prize lecture, which discusses the difficulties associated with detecting a graviton. However, the fundamentals of quantizing gravity are discussed in many of the better textbooks; the one that happens to be right here on my desk at this very moment is an appropriate example, Gravitation by the late Thanu Padmanabhan. Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole? Yes, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon, but it requires a qualifier: We first need to decide what we mean by acceleration in this context. If you were to watch an object fall into a black hole, you’d see the following: As the object approaches the horizon, anything and everything will appear to slow down from your perspective. The object would become invisible as a matter of fact because all signals coming from it would be subject to exponentially increasing redshift, making those signals effectively undetectable. But assuming that nonetheless, you can continue to track the object’s motion, you’d find that it never actually reaches the horizon: From your perspective, its motion will appear to freeze, the moment of it reaching the horizon (indeed, the moment the horizon itself forms in the first place!) forever remaining in your future. If you were to fall freely into a black hole, you would of course feel no acceleration. You might feel tidal forces because different parts of your body would try to follow different trajectories: If the black hole is small (and by “small”, I mean any size smaller than the largest supermassive black holes) these tidal forces would in fact rip your body to shreds. But if the black hole is large enough, you might survive reaching, and getting past, the horizon (ignoring quantum behavior here and the role played by Hawking radiation). And at no point would you feel acceleration: you would be in free fall all this time. However! Suppose you are testing your Almost Infinitely Powerful Rocket (tm), by trying to hover as close to the event horizon as possible. You will find that the closer you are to the event horizon, the more force you need to stay in position. In fact, soon enough you’d be quashed inside your rocket, so perhaps it might be wise to just send an unmanned probe instead. The bottom line: you will find that no matter how powerful your rocket it, there’s a point near the event horizon where it’s just not powerful enough to stay hovering. At the event horizon proper, the rocket would need to be infinitely powerful, i.e., subjected to infinite acceleration, in order to stay motionless, and that, of course, is impossible. So yes, as I said, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon: It would take an Infinitely Powerful Rocket (which cannot exist) to overcome gravity at the horizon proper and just hover.

Would the first light in the universe early on "at average" traverse distances at another rate than now, because of the more frequent bending by gravity in a denser universe? No, there would be no significant “bending” except for light rays that happen to pass too close to massive, compact mass concentrations too often. In terms of the average, it’s helpful to keep in mind that what dominates gravity in the nonrelativistic limit is time dilation, not the change in spatial geometry. A light ray coming from the surface of a compact, massive object will appear redshifted to an observer in space, because clocks on that surface tick slower than identical clocks in deep space. Similarly, light coming from the distant past appears redshifted, in part, because the average gravitational field was greater back when matter was much denser. (Another reason is the Doppler redshift due to the rate of expansion itself, but at deep cosmological distances, time dilation dominates over Doppler.) As to the matter of distances, that concept becomes very tricky on its own right! When objects are nearby and their distance remains unchanged or changes slowly, we can measure that distance more or less directly by the exchange of light rays. But over cosmological distances, that is not necessarily possible even in principle; you may send a light ray to a high-redshift, distant galaxy, but you will never observe that light ray catch up with that galaxy, so there will be no response. In the absence of such a direct measurement even in the form of a thought experiment, we must resort to other definitions of “distance”: e.g., distance deduced from the luminosity of the object or distance deduced from the angular size of that object. These inferred quantities are at best poor substitutes for what you or I would consider “distance” in our intuition. In light of this perhaps it makes a tad more sense when someone tells you that, e.g., a high-redshift galaxy was “only” a few billion light years from here when its light was emitted; that light nonetheless traveled for more than ten billion years (so the “light travel distance” is in excess of ten billion light years); and that at the present day, the so-called “comoving distance” to that object is several ten billion light years. All these numbers are valid; none of these numbers describe an ordinary, “sensible” distance, as no such distance can be measured. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Stuff can escape from the event horizon if it collides with another? But all the mass-energy of colliding black holes is not contained within their event horizons. You forgot about gravitational potential energy between the two black holes. Gravitational potential energy is zero when the black holes are very far apart, not interacting. As they get closer, that gravitational potential energy, which is negative (!), increases in magnitude. Since energy is conserved, this increase in negative potential energy must be accompanied by a corresponding increase in something positive. In this case, that something positive is the kinetic energy of the black holes accelerating towards each other. Now if the black holes were to collide head-on, this would be the end of the story: after the collision, the merged black hole would absorb all that kinetic energy. The total mass-energy of the system would be the same as before the collision: the sum of the masses of the progenitor black holes. But if the black holes approach each other off-center, they don’t collide right away. Rather, they will enter inspiraling orbits. This will produce gravitational radiation. The energy of that gravitational radiation will come at the expense of the kinetic energies of the inspiraling black holes. Now you’d think that would slow them down but orbital mechanics is tricky: as they lose energy, they enter into an ever tighter orbit, actually speeding up! This runaway process results in a gradual increase of the rate at which gravitational radiation is produced, reaching a final crescendo as the black holes get close enough to merge. Once the merger begins, the process rapidly comes to an end: a short “ringdown” phase occurs and the merger is complete. But in the meantime, a substantial amount of that gravitational potential energy, turned kinetic energy, is released as gravitational radiation and never becomes part of the mass-energy of the merged black hole. And in case you are wondering about actual, physical black holes that never quite reach the stage (as seen by us, outside observers) of forming actual event horizons, that makes no difference: though the respective event horizons remain forever in our future, the “asymptotic” behavior of the black holes is observationally indistinguishable from that hypothetical end state. Long story short: gravitational potential energy turns into kinetic energy that — in case of an off-center approach — turns into gravitational radiation before the merger is complete. From an outside observers point of view, a black hole never forms. The rest of the universe is an outside observer. So how can Hawking radiation ever escape to the outside universe? As others pointed out, the popular account of Hawking radiation — a pair of particles popping into existence near the event horizon, one with positive one with negative energy, the negative energy particle being “eaten” by the horizon while the other escapes — is dead wrong. In fact, we can suspect this much simply by looking at the basic features of Hawking radiation. Its characteristic wavelength is about 20 times (!) the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. That alone should make it fairly obvious that Hawking radiation doesn’t really come from the horizon proper. Indeed, when we actually look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper (rather than his popular book) a very different picture emerges. Hawking radiation is deduced from a so-called semiclassical description of quantum fields: that is to say, quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of general relativity. This curved spacetime background is not static. An astrophysical black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This creates an asymmetry between past and future. When we extend the quantum fields using the appropriate “past infinity” and “future infinity” boundary conditions, the resulting configuration is not symmetric. This yields an outgoing flow of radiation, which is what Hawking radiation really is. This radiation originates from the neighborhood of the gravitating object, and it is a result of the “gravitational vacuum polarization” that is produced by the object’s gravitational field. The presence of a horizon is not essential to this process, nor does the radiation originate from, or from within, the horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the difference in difficulty between quantum mechanics and quantum field theory? Why is one considered easier than the other? I don’t know about “easier”… understanding the quantum world is not easy, because it does not lend itself to intuition. This obstacle is the same whether you do field theory or particle theory. A particle theory in classical mechanics deals with the positions and momenta of particles subject to forces, which may be represented by potentials. We may turn a classical particle theory into a quantum theory by replacing positions and momenta with abstract entities that do not commute under multiplication. These abstract entities, “q-numbers” as Dirac called them, can be represented by matrices or by operators acting on some function, which represents the state of the system. The resulting equation (Schrödinger’s) is already known as a wave equation (that is to say, its solutions are typically wave-like solutions) so the function representing the state of the system is called the wavefunction. In the standard (Copenhagen) interpretation, we view this wavefunction as a probability density, as the squared norm of this function can be used to calculate the outcome of measurements, taken by (idealized, hypothesized) classical instruments. When we take the Schrödinger equation for a specific system known from classical mechanics, the harmonic oscillator, the solutions we get have a peculiar property: Only certain, discrete levels of energy represent valid solutions. This is an example of a system that became “quantized”. (As I hope it is obvious from the discussion so far, not all quantum systems are “quantized” in this sense of the word! E.g., a free particle can have any energy, its energy levels are not “quantized” even in the quantum theory.) So what is a field? In classical physics, a field is a physical entity that is present at every location at every moment in time. The field’s value may change from point to point or moment to moment, but it is governed by some sensible equation. In particular, we can assign for instance a “momentum density” to the field at various points, and use it to study how the field evolves over time. But there is one other thing that we can do with a field: Express it as a sum of elementary sine waves by means of a Fourier-transform. And elementary sine waves are basically harmonic oscillators! This, then, opens a path towards quantizing fields: If we can express a field as a (potentially infinite) sum of harmonic oscillators, we know already how to quantize harmonic oscillators. There, we have a quantum field theory. Now each of these harmonic oscillators has discrete energy levels. Its energy can only go up or down by set units. The premise of quantum field theory is that it is these discrete units that we perceive as particles. So when we say, for instance, that the electromagnetic field is “quantized” and its quanta are the “photons”, this is exactly what happens: Each “photon” is a unit excitation of one of the (infinitely many) harmonic oscillators that make up the electromagnetic field in this representation. Why do we do this, you might wonder? Well, quantum field theory has two very important properties that make all this effort worthwhile. First, as it allows the field to gain, or lose, excitations when it interacts with other fields, it lets us model particle creation and annihilation. No quantum particle theory can do that. And of course we do observe in Nature particle creation and annihilation all the time. Secondly, a quantum particle theory is known to violate causality. No matter how clever we are, constructing a relativistic version of quantum mechanics, there is always some “probability leakage” (my expression), some small but nonvanishing probability of an event influencing another event faster than light, or worse, backwards in time. In turn, quantum field theory is strictly causal: Such acausal interactions are exactly canceled out by the theory, no “leakage”. So why do people think quantum field theory is only an “effective” theory then? Well, I mentioned those pesky harmonic oscillators. Their energy levels are not only discrete, their lowest energy level is not zero! Now this is not a problem when all you have is one harmonic oscillator. But a field consists of infinitely many of them. Infinitely many oscillators means an infinite amount of “zero point energy”, which does not make sense. It turns out that in many cases, these infinities can be dealt with using a reasonably robust mathematical procedure, allowing us to extract finite numbers that describe actual observable results. The mathematical process is called renormalization. But not all quantum field theories are renormalizable, and in particular, gravity is a theory that becomes non-renormalizable as a quantum field theory. Gravity becomes important for quantum systems at the “Planck scale”. So it is widely thought that at that energy scale, quantum field theory ceases to work, and something more fundamental is needed. So there, that sums it up. Does this make quantum field theory harder than quantum mechanics? Well, it certainly builds upon quantum mechanics. But in a sense, it “completes” quantum mechanics in a very sensible way, so perhaps conceptually it is easier, even if its mathematical toolset may be a tad more complicated. Then again, with the problem of renormalizability… perhaps it’s harder after all. You be the judge. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.
